title: To be realized
hookLine: the third truth's task is to be tasted for oneself (SN 56.11)

cards: Try explaining salt to someone who has never tasted it. It's white. It comes in crystals.
It makes food taste more like itself. None of that is salt. Then you put a pinch on their tongue, and in half a second they know more than every sentence you said.
Some things can be described, and some can only be tasted. The first sermon puts the third truth, the ending of craving, firmly in the second group, and elsewhere the Buddha uses salt to say so.

teach.h: SACCHIKĀTABBA: SEEN WITH YOUR OWN EYES.
teach.b: Two tasks so far: dukkha is to be understood, craving is to be let go. The third: the ending of craving is sacchikātabba, to be realized.
Pali dictionaries build the word from sacchi, before your own eyes, and a verb for making. Made real for yourself, witnessed in person. Not believed on someone's say-so, not admired from a distance.
The suttas have a word for the teaching that fits: ehipassiko, come and see. The Buddha doesn't ask anyone to accept the third truth because he said it. He says it can be seen.
Now the salt. In the Numbered Discourses, Paharada, a lord of the titans, tells the Buddha what the titans love about the ocean.
One of its wonders, he says, is that the great ocean has one taste, the taste of salt. The Buddha answers that just so, this teaching and discipline has one taste, the taste of freedom.
Wherever you dip in, the generosity, the precepts, the meditation, the stories, the taste is meant to be the same. So freedom isn't only at the far end of the path, in some final moment.
It's a taste, and tastes come in small amounts: a moment when resentment falls away, a morning when you're not chasing anything.
Some teachers say those small tastes matter, because they show the third truth isn't just a theory. They're also clear that a pinch isn't the whole ocean.

how: Buddhists often recite the qualities of the Dhamma, including that it is to be seen here and now and invites one to come and see; teachers stress testing the teaching in one's own experience.

o: to be taken on trust from a teacher
to be argued out in a debate
to be realized, seen for yourself

games.q: match the pieces of the third truth's task.
p: to be realized, seen for yourself
one taste, the taste of salt
one taste, the taste of freedom

s: the third truth is to be accepted on the Buddha's word
its task is to be realized, seen with your own eyes; the teaching is 'come and see'.
the Buddha told Paharada the teaching has one taste, freedom
as the ocean has one taste, salt, so the teaching has one taste, freedom.
a small taste of ease is the whole of nibbana
teachers say small tastes matter, and also that a pinch isn't the whole ocean.

games.q: you're Paharada, lord of the titans, telling the Buddha about the ocean's wonders. he replies about his teaching. what does he say its one taste is?
games.why: the ocean has one taste, salt; the teaching and discipline has one taste, freedom.

practice: Don't try to manufacture calm; look for a place where peace is already present: the stillness of your hands, the quiet between two sounds, the pause at the bottom of an out-breath.
When you find one, stay with it, the way you'd let a flavor sit on your tongue. If it slips away, look for the next one.

wordCard.voice: Sacchikātabba. To be realized, made real for yourself with your own eyes, the way the ocean's one taste is salt.

orig.note: Pali sacchikātabba: to be realized, made real with one's own eyes; the third truth's task.

carryVoice: Your line: taste it. Some things are only known by tasting. Day three hundred forty-one, done.
